fichas.title: Supporting Slopes
fichas.summary: Illustrates biological and structural techniques for supporting slopes, including living and dead fascines, pegged or stacked turfs, bush layering, anchored steel mesh, and stone or ballast support. Planted retaining walls can create usable space and accommodate considerable height differences; high walls may use ground anchors.
uses: Creating usable land beside roads and paths

dimensions.label: Pegged turf slope ratio
dimensions.context: The illustrated pegged turfs support slopes at a ratio of at least 1:2.
dimensions.ocr_raw:
BIOLOGICAL ENGINEERING
Supporting Slopes and Riverbanks

0 Living fascines

Planted retaining walls create room for usable properties, roads
and paths. Considerable height differences can be overcome.
Depending on the system and the slope, high walls can also be
built with ground anchors ~ 0.

f) Dead fascines

Supporting riverbanks
While, in the design of slope support, earth pressure and gravity
are the forces to be considered, the design of riverbank support
also has to take into account the effect of water and wave impact.
The optimal riverbank protection is a natural vegetation profile
next to the flowing water ~ 4!!) and healthy root systems prevent
the bank being damaged by wave impact.
There are many methods of protecting against erosion, particularly
the area above and below the waterline, which is most subject to
wave impact, e.g. bundles of willow fascines, rhizome edgings or
brush mattresses are possible.

fichas.title: Supporting Riverbanks
fichas.summary: Riverbank support must account for earth pressure, gravity, water, and wave impact. The page presents drainage and support methods using stone and ballast, stone packing, filters, ribs, and gabions, alongside natural vegetation profiles and root systems for erosion and wave-impact protection.

fichas.title: Vegetation Profile of a River Bank
fichas.summary: A riverbank cross-section relates vegetation zones and plant species to water levels and durations of inundation. The diagram labels highest, high, normal, and low water levels and shows plant communities ranging from softwood to hardwood zones.
uses: Selecting vegetation according to water-level exposure
